beats.text: This is me finishing my second shift of the day. Sixteen hours. My feet feel like two angry bricks.
And this is my landlord. Right now he is asleep. And tonight he is making more money than me.
He's asleep.
My grandpa always told me work hard and you'll be fine. And he wasn't lying. In his time it was true.
By the end of this video you'll know the exact moment hard work stopped paying and the one switch that puts you on the other side.
But most people never find out because they're too tired to finish the video. Which is kind of the whole point.
So let me tell you about grandpa's deal. He worked at a factory. One job. Forty hours a week.
With that one paycheck he bought a house. A car. He fed four kids. And grandma didn't even have to work if she didn't want to.
Grandma still talks about their first color TV like it was a moon landing. They paid cash. Cash. Who pays cash for anything?
Me hearing that one paycheck bought a house and a car and four kids.
He wasn't a genius. He wasn't lucky. He just worked. And every year the company made more stuff and grandpa got a bigger slice.
That was the deal back then. If the factory got better at making stuff the workers got richer too. The boss and the worker climbed the stairs together.
When the company had a great year there was a Christmas bonus and a turkey for every family. A whole turkey. My job gave me a mug.

Ever. Not lowest this year. Lowest since they started counting.

Workers looking for their share of the pie.
So what changed? A bunch of things at once. Unions shrank. Jobs moved to cheaper countries. Machines replaced people. And companies started caring about one person above everyone else.
Back in grandpa's day a big chunk of factory workers were in a union. Today it's way fewer. Fewer people at the table means a smaller slice when the pie gets cut.
The shareholder. The person who owns a piece of the company. Keeping them happy became job number one.
Companies deciding where the extra money goes.

So when a company makes a big profit it often buys back its own shares. That pushes the price up for the owners. Your raise? Maybe next year.
That's the moment hard work stopped making people rich. Not because work got easier. Because the reward for work stopped growing.
And here's the part that kept me awake. Money itself got a better deal than people.
Think about my landlord again. I work all month. Half my paycheck goes to him. He does nothing. And every year his building is worth more.
My landlord on the first of the month.
The people who owned stocks and buildings and businesses watched their stuff grow way faster than any paycheck. While they slept.
Since grandpa's time the stock market grew way faster than paychecks. Way faster. If you owned a piece of it you were pulled up. If you didn't you just watched.
There are two kinds of money. Money you earn with your body. And money your money earns. The first one gets tired. The second one never sleeps.
You can only work twenty four hours a day. Trust me I've tried. But money can work in a thousand places at once.
My landlord made more money this year by doing nothing than I made by delivering four hundred tacos. I counted. It was four hundred and twelve.
It's like a race where you run on your legs and the other guy rides an escalator that keeps getting faster. You can run harder. You won't catch him.
And the worst part? The escalator guy isn't smarter than you. He's not working harder than you. He just got on earlier.
Me running after the escalator guy.
And the gap feeds itself. The more you own the more you earn. The more you earn the more you buy. That's why it feels like the rich get richer on autopilot.

That's why the gap between owners and workers isn't just a gap. It's a gap that grows every single night while you sleep.
Remember the billionaire video? Same idea. They don't get rich from salary. They get rich from owning things.

Grandpa finding out his house did more work than him.

Me buying my first tiny slice of every company in the country.

People skipping the free match.
